questions.q: A patient has damage to the intestinal brush border but preserved pancreatic amylase secretion. Which step of carbohydrate digestion is most directly impaired?
options: Initial hydrolysis of starch in the intestinal lumen
Final hydrolysis of disaccharides to absorbable monosaccharides
Transport of glucose from the intestinal lumen into enterocytes by SGLT1
Delivery of glucose from enterocytes into portal blood
questions.explain: Pancreatic amylase produces oligosaccharides and disaccharides, but brush-border enzymes such as maltase, sucrase-isomaltase and lactase complete hydrolysis to monosaccharides. Brush-border injury therefore impairs this final digestive step.

questions.q: A patient with obstructed bile flow develops steatorrhoea despite adequate pancreatic lipase secretion. Which process is most directly impaired?
options: Emulsification and formation of mixed micelles that deliver lipid digestion products to the brush border
Hydrolysis of triglycerides by pancreatic lipase
Absorption of short-chain fatty acids directly into portal blood
questions.explain: Bile salts emulsify dietary fat and form mixed micelles that keep fatty acids and monoglycerides soluble in the intestinal lumen and deliver them to the brush border. Reduced bile delivery impairs lipid absorption and can cause steatorrhoea even when pancreatic lipase is present.

questions.q: A patient with brush-border damage has reduced absorption of glucose and galactose but relatively preserved fructose absorption. Which transporter is most likely impaired?
questions.explain: Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes apically through sodium-dependent SGLT1. Fructose uses GLUT5; monosaccharides leave basolaterally mainly through GLUT2.

open.q: Which apical transporter mediates sodium-dependent uptake of glucose and galactose?

questions.q: Which pancreatic zymogen is activated in the duodenal lumen by enteropeptidase?
questions.explain: Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border converts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates several other pancreatic zymogens.

open.q: Which pancreatic zymogen is activated by enteropeptidase?

questions.q: Most dietary dipeptides and tripeptides enter small-intestinal enterocytes across the apical membrane through which transporter?
options: PEPT1, coupled to the proton gradient
questions.explain: PEPT1 is a proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter on the apical membrane of small-intestinal enterocytes. It absorbs many dipeptides and tripeptides, which are then hydrolysed intracellularly to amino acids. Free amino acids use several distinct sodium-dependent or sodium-independent transport systems.

open.q: Which apical transporter absorbs most dietary dipeptides and tripeptides into small-intestinal enterocytes?

questions.q: A patient with a rare defect in intestinal fructose transport develops diarrhoea after consuming fruit juice, while glucose absorption remains intact. Which apical transporter is most likely defective?
questions.explain: Fructose enters small-intestinal enterocytes across the apical membrane by facilitated diffusion through GLUT5. Glucose and galactose use the sodium-dependent cotransporter SGLT1. GLUT2 normally mediates basolateral exit of monosaccharides.

open.q: Which apical transporter mediates fructose uptake by small-intestinal enterocytes?

questions.q: After glucose and galactose enter an enterocyte from the intestinal lumen, through which transporter do they normally leave across the basolateral membrane to enter portal blood?
questions.explain: Glucose, galactose and fructose leave enterocytes across the basolateral membrane mainly through GLUT2 by facilitated diffusion. The Na+/K+-ATPase maintains the sodium gradient that drives apical SGLT1-mediated glucose and galactose uptake.

open.q: Which transporter mediates basolateral exit of absorbed monosaccharides from enterocytes?

questions.q: A patient undergoes surgical resection of the terminal ileum and later develops vitamin B12 deficiency. Which complex is normally taken up by specific receptors in this region?
options: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor
Vitamin B12 bound to transcobalamin II
Free vitamin B12 bound to albumin
Vitamin B12 bound to haptocorrin in the stomach
questions.explain: In the stomach, vitamin B12 is released from food and ultimately binds intrinsic factor secreted by parietal cells. The intrinsic factor–B12 complex binds cubilin-related receptors in the terminal ileum and is taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

open.q: In which form is vitamin B12 absorbed by receptor-mediated uptake in the terminal ileum?
accept: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor

questions.q: A patient with disease affecting the terminal ileum loses large quantities of bile salts in faeces. Which normal transport process is most directly impaired?
options: Passive diffusion of bile salts throughout the stomach
Active sodium-dependent reabsorption of bile acids in the terminal ileum
SGLT1-mediated uptake of bile salts in the jejunum
Intrinsic factor-mediated uptake of bile salts in the colon
questions.explain: Conjugated bile acids are efficiently reclaimed in the terminal ileum by the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT). Ileal disease or resection disrupts enterohepatic circulation, reducing the bile salt pool and potentially causing fat malabsorption.

open.q: Which transporter is responsible for active reabsorption of conjugated bile acids in the terminal ileum?

questions.q: A patient with iron deficiency has reduced absorption of non-haem iron from the duodenal lumen. Which apical transporter normally carries ferrous iron (Fe2+) into enterocytes?
questions.explain: Dietary non-haem ferric iron (Fe3+) is reduced to ferrous iron (Fe2+) at the brush border and enters duodenal enterocytes through DMT1. Ferroportin exports iron across the basolateral membrane, while hepcidin regulates ferroportin availability.

open.q: Which apical transporter takes up ferrous iron into duodenal enterocytes?
